segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants gave us tat, that: a pointing word that waits a line for its noun. Today, the word that says whose.

Phones come out at sunrise on any beach, and not everyone agrees on what they're photographing. Some see the sun. Some see what the sun stands for. Readers of the Gayatri have split the same way for a long time. Its second word is savitur, of Savitr. Is that the sun in the sky, or something the sun only hints at? The honest answer: inside the tradition, both readings have their defenders. Here are both, at their best.
screen: `SAVITUR: OF SAVITR.` → `THE SUN, OR BEHIND IT?`

segments.voice: First the grammar, because both sides stand on it. The god's name is Savitr. The verse says savitur. Two layers sit on the name. The ending makes it savituh, of Savitr, Savitr's. Then a sound join: before the v of varenyam, that final breath becomes r. So a reader peels twice and finds the name underneath. The radiance belongs to Savitr. The verse doesn't say more about who he is. Now the first view. In the Rig Veda's hymns, Savitr is the god of the sun's going: the one who rouses the day and sets things moving. So some families say the Gayatri facing the rising sun, at the joining times of the day, and hear in it the real light of a real morning. Its strength: it keeps the verse in the body, at a window, under an actual sky. The second view. Some teachers who read the Upanishads hear Savitr's radiance as an inner light, the light by which the mind sees anything at all, sun included. Its strength: it explains why the verse asks for thoughts to be stirred, not crops to grow. The grammar holds both. Of Savitr says whose the radiance is. It leaves the rest to the reader.
screen: `SAVITUH + A JOIN = SAVITUR.` · `VIEW ONE: THE SUN'S OWN LIGHT.` · `VIEW TWO: A LIGHT BEHIND SEEING.` · `THE GRAMMAR HOLDS BOTH.` · then, large: `WHOSE, NOT WHAT.`

segments.voice: Turn your body toward the brightest direction near you, a window or a lamp, and sit tall with your palms resting on your knees. Feel the light on your face for a few breaths. Then, still facing it, notice the seeing itself, the part of you that knows there's light.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: savitur, of Savitr, the word that says whose radiance it is.

fork.setup: Sam says the Gayatri is 'basically a sun prayer, nothing deeper.' Priya disagrees. before she answers, what's the best case for Sam's side?

fork.reveal: Sam's best case stands on the hymns: Savitr is the god of the sun's going, and the verse is said toward the light. the inner reading has its own best case. the grammar leaves room for both.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: Savitr, the god whose radiance the Gayatri holds in mind; savitur means of Savitr.

what a scholar hears: savituḥ is a genitive; its final breath turns to r before the voiced v of vareṇyam, and readers since have heard Savitr as the sun and as an inner light.
